description:
Hey! We're building an interactive 3D map of the Moon's south pole that shows the best places to land: where there's sunlight to power a base and a clear view of Earth to stay in touch with home.

We're looking for people who like coding, design, or presenting. No space experience needed, just curiosity and good vibes. Join us! 🚀🌙
summary: Aripi is a web app that answers one question for a Moon south-pole mission: where and when can a lander land and survive? At the pole the Sun circles about 1 degree above the horizon, so a crater rim kilometres away decides whether a spacecraft has power and a direct line to Earth. For any site and any landing day from 2026 to 2035, Aripi checks the Sun and the Earth against the real terrain horizon computed from NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL Horizons positions. The lead view is a landing-window calendar: pick a site, set your limits (mission length, sunlight, Earth contact, longest night), and every day shows whether it works and why. When a launch slips, every landing day is re-checked in seconds. It also shows permanently shadowed regions and other missions' hardware. Our results match NASA's own sunlight and Earth-visibility maps (r = 0.993 at NASA's resolution).
details:
WHO IT IS FOR

Teams in the early planning stage of a south-pole landing (concept studies, proposals, future CLPS-style missions) who need to know which spots and which weeks give their spacecraft enough sunlight and Earth contact, and who must re-check that in seconds when the launch slips. The same view shows students and the public why the lunar south pole is hard. It is a comparison and screening tool for many options, not a flight-planning tool.

WHAT IT DOES

At the south pole the Sun circles close to the horizon and the Earth bobs up and down near it, so a crater rim a few kilometres away can decide whether a lander has power and a direct line to Earth. For every site and date the tool checks the Sun and the Earth against the real terrain horizon computed from NASA LOLA elevation data.

- Landing-window calendar (lead view): one cell per landing day, good day to land or not, with the reason and the numbers in plain words (e.g. "not enough sunlight (66%, you need 70%)").

- Your limits as sliders: mission length, minimum sunlight, minimum Earth contact, longest night, Sun above the horizon at touchdown. Presets are example values, not NASA requirements.

- Time span 1 to 5 years from any start date (2026-2036). Compare sites ranked by good landing days.

- Right now at a site: time to sunset/sunrise and Earthset/Earthrise, a horizon chart, and 3D LOLA terrain lit by the real Sun.

- Mast height 0/2/10 m; relay switch; distance to permanent shadow (a model, not a map of ice); other missions' hardware with a keep-out filter (NASA 2011 non-binding guidance).

- Team terrain analysis (ArcGIS): 16 flat, smooth areas; our light engine found flat spots with 60-72% sun inside them.

- Missions view: fly a chosen day from Spaceport Nova Scotia, a simplified flight model, touchdown and the sky during the stay.

HOW IT WORKS

Offline (Python): for each site a 360-direction terrain horizon from 20 m LOLA terrain near the site and 80 m beyond, Moon curvature included; rays stop automatically once no terrain can rise above the horizon already found. 1,531 permanently shadowed regions from NASA PGDA product 90.

In the browser (JavaScript): Sun and Earth directions from a JPL Horizons table (2026-2036), checked against the site's horizon every hour. No atmosphere, so the horizon is only terrain.

VALIDATION (our own tests)

- Page vs an independent Python engine: 10,589 of 10,590 landing days agree.

- Sun position vs JPL Horizons at the site: within 0.0003 degrees.

- Against NASA's own long-run sunlight and Earth-visibility maps (PGDA product 69): r = 0.993 at NASA's resolution.

- Shackleton rim: 79.1% sunlight vs 81.0% published (Glaser et al. 2018).

IMPACT AND CREATIVITY

Existing NASA tools are built for detailed analysis of one point or for averages. We turn the same public data into an answer you can check in seconds: which spots and which weeks work, and why. When a launch slips, the whole calendar is re-checked at once.

LIMITS

Geometry only: no battery, thermal, radio link budget or landing-hazard model. Not a NASA product and not a flight tool.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj), JavaScript and three.js, JPL Horizons API, GitHub Pages.

Code: https://github.com/erenhocoklu/Peaks-of-Light-Lunar-Landing-Site-Navigator

Live app: https://erenhocoklu.github.io/Peaks-of-Light-Lunar-Landing-Site-Navigator/
